read.glossary.2.word.note: "State" is "negara", which learners also read as "country". The definition keeps the English meaning (people in one area under one government). Check it doesn't suggest modern countries.

read.glossary.3.word.note: "Law" is "hukum". "Undang-undang" is also possible; "hukum" is shorter and used for Hammurabi's laws. "sekitar 280 hukum" may sound slightly odd; "280 pasal hukum" is an alternative.

read.sections.0.text.note: "priests" is "pendeta", the usual word for ancient priests in history books, but in daily use it means a Christian pastor. "farming towns" is "permukiman petani" to avoid "kota" twice with two meanings.
read.sections.0.text.back: More than 5,000 years ago, some farming settlements grew into the first cities. One of the earliest was Uruk, in Mesopotamia, in the area that is now Iraq. Other early cities grew on the banks of the Nile River in Egypt and the Indus River in South Asia. Some also grew in the Yellow River valley in China. Later, cities also grew in Mexico, Central America and West Africa. Every city needed a food surplus. With extra food, thousands of people could eat without having to farm. Then many people could specialise in one kind of work. They became builders, potters, traders or priests. In Banwa, extra grain let potters, builders and record-keepers each have one main job.
read.sections.0.text.source: More than 5,000 years ago, some farming towns grew into the first cities. One of the earliest was Uruk, in Mesopotamia, in what is now Iraq. Other early cities grew beside the Nile in Egypt and the Indus River in South Asia. Some grew in the Yellow River valley in China. Later, cities also grew in Mexico, Central America and West Africa. Every city needed a food surplus. With extra food, thousands of people could eat without farming. Then many people could specialise in one kind of work. They became builders, potters, traders or priests. In Banwa, extra grain lets potters, builders and record keepers each do one main job.

read.sections.1.text.note: "Babylon" is "Babilonia". "had about 280 laws carved" is "membuat sekitar 280 hukum yang dipahat" so it doesn't say the king carved them himself.
read.sections.1.text.back: Many cities became part of a state. A state is a group of people in one area led by one government. Rulers and officials made decisions for everyone and settled disputes. They also made laws, that is, rules everyone must follow. In Babylon, King Hammurabi made about 280 laws carved on a tall black stone. States also collected taxes, and people often paid them with grain, animals or labour. In Egypt, farmers gave part of their harvest to the ruler. Taxes were used to pay for canals, walls, storehouses and temples. In Banwa, the leaders organised the building of canals and made rules about water.
read.sections.1.text.source: Many cities became part of a state. A state is a group of people in one area who are led by one government. Rulers and officials made choices for everyone and settled arguments. They also made laws, which are rules that everyone must follow. In Babylon, King Hammurabi had about 280 laws carved on a tall black stone. States collected taxes too, and people often paid in grain, animals or work. In Egypt, farmers gave part of their harvest to the ruler. Taxes paid for canals, walls, storehouses and temples. In Banwa, leaders organise a canal and make rules about the water.

watch.summary.back: This video tells about ancient Egypt, one of the world's early states. The Nile River flows through a dry desert. Every year, the river flooded and left fertile soil on its banks. Farmers used this soil to grow a great deal of grain. That surplus fed many people who did other work, like builders, craftspeople and scribes who wrote records. The Nile was also like a road. Boats carried food, stone and other goods upstream and downstream. Egypt was ruled by kings called pharaohs, with many officials helping them. They collected taxes, planned work and made records. Because of that, Egypt could build very large projects. But power was not shared equally. Egypt is just one example. Other early cities and states grew in different ways.
watch.summary.source: This video tells the story of ancient Egypt, one of the world's early states. The Nile River runs through a dry desert. Each year, the river flooded and left rich soil on its banks. Farmers used this soil to grow large amounts of grain. The surplus fed many people who did other work, such as builders, craftspeople and scribes, who wrote records. The Nile was also like a road. Boats carried food, stone and other goods up and down the river. Egypt was ruled by kings called pharaohs, with many officials to help them. They collected taxes, planned work and kept records. This let Egypt build huge projects. But power was not shared equally. Egypt is only one example. Other early cities and states grew in different ways.

read.sections.2.text.back: To collect taxes and share out food, officials had to remember and count many things. So some early states started making written records. In Mesopotamia, people pressed marks into wet clay to count grain and animals. Egypt, China and the Maya people in Central America also made their own writing. The Indus cities also had signs, but until now nobody has been able to read them. By working together, a city could build things that one family could not build. But power was not shared equally. Rulers, officials and rich families often controlled land, grain and water. Some laws protected ordinary people, but other laws benefited the powerful more.
read.sections.2.text.source: To collect taxes and share out food, officials needed to keep track of a lot. So some early states began to keep a record in writing. In Mesopotamia, people pressed marks into wet clay to count grain and animals. Egypt, China and the Maya of Central America also made their own writing. The Indus cities had signs too, but nobody can read them yet. Working together, a city could build things that one family could not. But power was not shared equally. Rulers, officials and rich families often controlled land, grain and water. Some laws protected people, but others helped the powerful more.

read.sections.2.simpler.back: The leaders needed to count a lot of grain. So some states started making written records. In the area that is now Iraq, people pressed marks into wet clay. That way, they counted grain. Egypt, China and the Maya people also made writing. Nobody can read the Indus signs yet. In a city, people could build big things together. But power was not shared fairly. Rulers and rich families often had more land and grain. Some laws helped rich people more.

write.example.back: Banwa started to change when its fields produced extra grain for several years. This meant people could build a big storehouse for that grain. Some people could stop farming and work as potters, builders or traders. Next, the leaders planned canals and made rules about water. Records helped because record-keepers could count grain and taxes. Some people got more power because they had more land and grain than other families.

Records helped because the record keeper could count the grain and the tax. Some people gained more power because they had more land and grain than other families.
